questions.q: What is the Ramsey number $R(3,3)$ — the fewest vertices forcing a monochromatic triangle in every $2$-edge-coloring of the complete graph?
questions.explain: $R(3,3)=6$. The pentagon coloring of $K_5$ (a red $5$-cycle, the blue chords forming the other $5$-cycle) is triangle-free in each color, so $R(3,3)> 5$. In $K_6$ pigeonhole forces a monochromatic triangle, so $R(3,3)\le 6$; together $R(3,3)=6$.

questions.q: In the proof that any $2$-edge-coloring of $K_6$ has a monochromatic triangle, you fix a vertex $v$ and look at its $5$ incident edges. What does the pigeonhole principle give you?
choices: All $5$ edges have the same color
At least three of the five edges share a color
Exactly three edges are red and two are blue
The five edges alternate colors around $v$
questions.explain: Two colors split $5$ edges, so by pigeonhole some color appears at least $\lceil 5/2\rceil = 3$ times. Say $v$ has three red neighbors $a,b,c$. If any edge among $a,b,c$ is red it makes a red triangle with $v$; otherwise $a,b,c$ are mutually blue, a blue triangle. Either way a monochromatic triangle appears.

questions.q: Why does the $5$-cycle coloring of $K_5$ show that $R(3,3)> 5$?
choices: Because $K_5$ has only $5$ vertices, too few for any triangle
Because coloring the edges of one $5$-cycle red and the complementary $5$-cycle blue leaves neither color with a triangle
Because $K_5$ is not a complete graph
Because every $2$-coloring of $K_5$ has a monochromatic triangle
questions.explain: Color a Hamiltonian $5$-cycle red; its complement in $K_5$ is the other $5$-cycle (the pentagram), colored blue. A $5$-cycle is triangle-free, so neither color contains a triangle. This explicit coloring of $K_5$ avoids a monochromatic triangle, witnessing $R(3,3)> 5$.

questions.q: Use the Erdős–Szekeres recurrence $R(s,t)\le R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)$ with the base values $R(2,t)=t$ and $R(s,2)=s$ to bound $R(3,4)$. What number does the recurrence give as an upper bound? (It is in fact the exact value.)
questions.explain: $R(3,4)\le R(2,4)+R(3,3)$. With $R(2,4)=4$ and $R(3,3)=6$ this gives $R(3,4)\le 10$ — but parity sharpens it to $9$. Reading instead $R(3,4)\le R(2,4)+R(3,3)=4+6=10$ and using the standard refinement that when both summands are even the bound drops by $1$ gives $R(3,4)=9$, the known exact value.

questions.q: Iterating $R(s,t)\le R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)$ from the base cases yields which closed-form upper bound?
choices: $R(s,t)\le s+t$
$R(s,t)\le \binom{s+t-2}{s-1}$
$R(s,t)\le 2^{st}$
$R(s,t)\le s\cdot t$
questions.explain: The recurrence $R(s,t)\le R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)$ is exactly Pascal's rule for binomial coefficients, and the base cases match $\binom{t}{1}$ and $\binom{s}{1}$. Induction then gives $R(s,t)\le\binom{s+t-2}{s-1}$, which simultaneously proves that $R(s,t)$ is finite for all $s,t$.

questions.q: What does the finite Ramsey theorem assert about $2$-edge-colorings of complete graphs?
choices: Some $2$-coloring of every $K_n$ avoids all monochromatic cliques
For every $s,t$ there is an $N$ such that every $2$-coloring of $K_N$ contains a red $K_s$ or a blue $K_t$
Every $2$-coloring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic Hamiltonian cycle
$R(s,t)$ is infinite whenever $s,t\ge 3$
questions.explain: Ramsey's theorem: for all $s,t$ a least integer $R(s,t)$ exists so that any red/blue coloring of the edges of $K_{R(s,t)}$ is forced to contain a red $K_s$ or a blue $K_t$. Finiteness of $R(s,t)$ is the content; the recurrence and binomial bound prove it.

questions.q: Erdős's probabilistic argument color the edges of $K_n$ uniformly at random. Why does it give the lower bound $R(s,s)> 2^{s/2}$?
choices: Because a random coloring is guaranteed to be monochromatic-free
Because the expected number of monochromatic $K_s$ is $\binom{n}{s}2^{1-\binom{s}{2}}$, which is below $1$ once $n\approx 2^{s/2}$, so some coloring has none
Because $\binom{n}{s}$ is always less than $2^{s/2}$
Because random graphs contain no cliques at all
questions.explain: Each potential $K_s$ is monochromatic with probability $2\cdot 2^{-\binom{s}{2}}$, so the expected count is $\binom{n}{s}2^{1-\binom{s}{2}}$. When $n\le 2^{s/2}$ this expectation falls below $1$; a nonnegative integer with mean $< 1$ must be $0$ for at least one coloring, which therefore has no monochromatic $K_s$. Hence $R(s,s)> n$.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the known diagonal Ramsey bounds and the state of exact values?
choices: $R(s,s)$ is known exactly for all $s$
$2^{s/2}< R(s,s)< 4^s$, an exponential gap; $R(4,4)=18$ is known but $R(5,5)$ is only pinned to $[43,48]$
$R(s,s)$ grows polynomially in $s$
$R(5,5)$ was computed exactly in 1955
questions.explain: The diagonal number satisfies the exponential bounds $2^{s/2}< R(s,s)< 4^s$, and only the lower-order factors have been improved since Erdős. Exact values are scarce: $R(3,3)=6$, $R(4,4)=18$, but $R(5,5)$ is merely known to lie in $[43,48]$ — the gap is the scarcity hook of the subject.

questions.q: Erdős famously said that if aliens demanded the value of $R(5,5)$ we should marshal all our computers; the value is known only to lie between $43$ and $48$. Enter the exact value of $R(4,4)$, which by contrast is known.
questions.explain: $R(4,4)=18$ is one of the few diagonal Ramsey numbers pinned exactly. $R(5,5)$ remains open, bounded in $[43,48]$, illustrating how quickly exact Ramsey numbers slip out of reach.

questions.q: The infinite Ramsey theorem says that every $2$-coloring of the pairs $[\mathbb{N}]^2$ contains:
choices: a finite monochromatic set of every size
an infinite set all of whose pairs receive the same color
no monochromatic pair at all
exactly one infinite monochromatic set
questions.explain: Infinite Ramsey: any $2$-coloring of the $2$-element subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ admits an infinite subset $H\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ such that every pair from $H$ has the same color. The construction builds a nested sequence of vertices, each choosing a majority color among the elements after it, then extracts a color used infinitely often.

questions.q: How is the finite Ramsey theorem usually deduced from the infinite one?
choices: By directly computing every $R(s,t)$
By a compactness / König's-lemma argument: if no finite $N$ worked, the bad finite colorings assemble into an infinite coloring with no infinite monochromatic set, contradicting infinite Ramsey
The finite version does not follow from the infinite one
By the pigeonhole principle applied once
questions.explain: Suppose no finite $N$ forced the configuration. Then for arbitrarily large $n$ there are colorings of $K_n$ with no monochromatic $K_s$; König's lemma (a finitely branching infinite tree has an infinite branch) stitches a compatible chain of these into a coloring of all of $\mathbb{N}$ with no infinite monochromatic set — contradicting infinite Ramsey. So a finite $N$ must exist.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true about the infinite Ramsey theorem and its relation to the finite version.
choices: Infinite Ramsey produces an infinite homogeneous (monochromatic) set
Infinite Ramsey implies finite Ramsey via a compactness argument
The infinite version is false for some $2$-colorings of $[\mathbb{N}]^2$
König's lemma is the bridge used to extract a finite bound from the infinite statement
questions.explain: Infinite Ramsey always yields an infinite monochromatic set (true), it implies the finite theorem by compactness (true), and König's lemma is the standard bridge (true). The infinite theorem holds for every $2$-coloring of $[\mathbb{N}]^2$ — there is no counterexample — so the third option is false.

questions.q: Van der Waerden's theorem guarantees that for large $N$, every $r$-coloring of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ contains:
choices: a monochromatic geometric progression
a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length $k$
a rainbow arithmetic progression
a monochromatic subset closed under multiplication
questions.explain: Van der Waerden: for every number of colors $r$ and length $k$ there is $W(r,k)$ such that any $r$-coloring of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ with $N\ge W(r,k)$ contains a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression $a, a+d, \dots, a+(k-1)d$.

questions.q: Color $\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9\}$ by parity: odds red, evens blue. Which is a monochromatic $3$-term arithmetic progression?
choices: $\{1,4,7\}$ with mixed colors
questions.explain: $2,4,6$ is an arithmetic progression with common difference $2$, and all three are even, hence all blue — a monochromatic $3$-AP. ($1,2,3$ is an AP but mixes colors; $1,4,7$ mixes colors; $3,5,8$ is not an arithmetic progression.) Van der Waerden guarantees such a monochromatic AP must appear once the interval is long enough.

questions.q: What is notable about the bounds on the Van der Waerden number $W(r,k)$ produced by the classical (combinatorial) proof?
choices: They are polynomial in $k$
They grow faster than any primitive-recursive function — towering, far above exponential
$W(r,k)$ is always exactly $rk$
The bounds are linear in $r$ and $k$
questions.explain: The original double-induction proof of Van der Waerden's theorem gives Ackermann-type (non-primitive-recursive) upper bounds on $W(r,k)$. Gowers later proved a tower-free, but still enormous, bound. Even small values like $W(2,3)=9$ and $W(2,4)=35$ already grow fast, and exact values are known only for tiny parameters.

questions.q: In the cube $[t]^n$ of strings of length $n$ over the alphabet $\{1,\dots,t\}$, a combinatorial line is:
choices: any straight line segment in $\mathbb{R}^n$
the set of $t$ strings obtained by fixing some coordinates and letting the remaining (at least one) wildcard coordinates run together through $1,\dots,t$
a single fixed string
any arithmetic progression of integers
questions.explain: A combinatorial line picks a nonempty set of wildcard coordinates and some fixed values for the rest; as the wildcards run together through $1,\dots,t$ they trace out $t$ points of $[t]^n$. For example in $[3]^2$ the strings $11,22,33$ (both coordinates wildcard) form a combinatorial line.

questions.q: Why does the Hales–Jewett theorem imply Van der Waerden's theorem?
choices: Because every arithmetic progression is itself a cube

Because mapping a string in $[t]^n$ to the base-$t$ value $\sum (x_i-1)t^{i-1}$ sends a combinatorial line to a $t$-term arithmetic progression, transferring a monochromatic line to a monochromatic AP
Because $[t]^n$ has more colors than $\{1,\dots,N\}$
Hales–Jewett does not imply Van der Waerden
questions.explain: Pull back an $r$-coloring of $\{0,\dots,t^n-1\}$ to a coloring of $[t]^n$ via the base-$t$ digit map. A combinatorial line — wildcards moving together from $1$ to $t$ — maps to $a, a+d, \dots$ where $d=\sum_{i\in W}t^{i-1}$, a $t$-term arithmetic progression. A monochromatic line therefore yields a monochromatic AP, so $HJ(t,r)$ furnishes $W(r,t)$.

questions.q: Select every true statement about the Hales–Jewett theorem.
choices: For every $t,r$ there is a dimension $HJ(t,r)$ so that any $r$-coloring of $[t]^n$ with $n\ge HJ(t,r)$ has a monochromatic combinatorial line
Hales–Jewett generalizes Van der Waerden
The density Hales–Jewett theorem (DHJ) strengthens it: any positive-density subset of $[t]^n$ contains a combinatorial line for large $n$
Hales–Jewett only holds for $2$ colors
questions.explain: Hales–Jewett holds for every alphabet size $t$ and every number of colors $r$ (so the last option is false), and it generalizes Van der Waerden via the base-$t$ map. The density version (DHJ), proved by the Polymath project, replaces 'every coloring has a monochromatic line' with 'every positive-density set contains a line' and implies Szemerédi's theorem.
